title: Understanding Teacher Revisions of Large Language Model-Generated Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers revise feedback generated by large language models (LLMs) before it is delivered to students. The central question is not whether the model can produce plausible feedback, but how educators actually mediate, edit, and sometimes accept that feedback in authentic instructional workflows. The authors frame teacher revision as a key part of evaluating AI feedback systems because it determines what learners ultimately receive.

The study analyzes 1,349 instances of AI-generated formative feedback paired with final teacher-edited versions from 117 teachers. The data came from Tutoria, an AI-supported feedback platform integrated with Moodle and Google Classroom, used in a mix of controlled studies and classroom deployments. Participants included Brazilian educators and students from multiple contexts, especially Brazilian high school chemistry and higher-education introductory computer science tasks involving short open-ended responses. Teachers could accept, edit, or rewrite LLM-generated drafts after tagging student responses for correctness.

The paper finds that teachers accepted the AI feedback unchanged in about 78% of cases, and when they did edit, they usually shortened the text while largely preserving its meaning. Editing varied greatly by teacher: over half never revised any feedback, while a small minority revised a large share. Text-only models could predict revision with above-chance accuracy, but only modestly. Qualitative coding showed that revisions often shifted feedback away from highly explanatory, high-information forms toward shorter corrective forms, suggesting that teachers frequently simplify overly verbose or pedagogically misaligned AI output. The authors conclude that default AI behavior is instructionally consequential because most feedback is delivered unchanged, and that future systems should better align with teacher preferences while reducing unnecessary editing burden.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical observational/quantitative study with descriptive, predictive, and coding analyses of real classroom logs, but it is not an experimental design and does not estimate causal effects on student learning. The evidence is informative for behavior in authentic use, yet credibility is limited by retrospective data and lack of outcome randomization.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests a potentially meaningful operational effect on teacher workload because 77.8% of AI feedback was accepted unchanged and revisions were usually brief, but it does not demonstrate learning gains or other direct educational impacts. Overall impact is therefore modest and somewhat unclear for general K-12 outcomes.

interventions.use_case: LLM-generated formative feedback for short open-ended student responses, with teachers able to accept, edit, or rewrite the draft before delivery

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that most AI-generated feedback was delivered unchanged, with teachers accepting drafts without modification in 77.8% of cases (1050/1349). Editing was limited and heterogeneous across teachers, suggesting the system may reduce teacher editing effort even though revised feedback was sometimes shortened by a mean of 6.4 words relative to the original draft.
finding.measure: Teacher revision rate; word counts of AI feedback vs final teacher feedback; semantic similarity between drafts and final messages
finding.std_deviation: AI feedback length SD=19.60; final feedback length SD=19.81

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on formative feedback for student writing/open-ended responses, but it does not measure learner writing outcomes directly. It does show that when teachers revised AI feedback, they often simplified high-information explanations into more concise corrective feedback, with revised messages shifting from 59.9% high-information at draft stage to 48.0% after editing (chi-square shift, Cramér’s V=0.12).
finding.measure: Feedback type coding of AI-generated and teacher-edited messages (corrective vs high-information vs reinforcement/punishment)
finding.study_size: n=834 deduplicated feedback messages coded; n=1349 logs overall
finding.effect_size: Cramér’s V=0.12; Cohen’s w=0.16-0.20 for distributional tests
